source_text:
ἔφθασεν; Εἰς τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Πατρὸς δηλονότι ἔφθασεν ὁ Υἱός. Καὶ πόθεν τοῦτο ἔστιν
ἰδεῖν, ἔφη πάλιν αὐτὸς ἐφεξῆς· Αὐτῷ ἐδόθη ἡ τιμὴ καὶ βασιλεία. Ἤκουσε γὰρ τοῦ
Πατρὸς λέγοντος· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν
ποδῶν σου.
thought_title: The Son reached the Father's glory
orientation: Cyril is answering his own question about how the Son's coming to the Ancient of Days is not spatial, by showing from Daniel and the Psalm that the Son entered the Father's glory.
pass_a_gloss: He reached? The Son clearly reached into the glory of the Father. And from where is this possible to see, he himself said again next: To him was given the honor and the kingdom. For he heard the Father saying: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.

choices.why: The verb φθάνω means to arrive at or reach a destination; here it answers the question of whether the Son's coming is spatial by saying he reached the Father's glory.
The adverb δηλονότι marks the answer as obvious or self-evident, reinforcing Cyril's rejection of the spatial reading.

choices.english: from where is this possible to see
choices.why: The interrogative πόθεν asks for the source or basis of the claim, and ἔστιν ἰδεῖν is an impersonal construction meaning 'it is possible to see.'
rejected: whence is this to be seen

choices.why: The adverb ἐφεξῆς means 'in sequence' or 'next,' indicating that the quotation from Daniel follows immediately in the text.
The construction ἕως ἄν with the subjunctive θῶ expresses a future condition: the sitting continues until the Father places the enemies as a footstool.

bible_refs.note: Αὐτῷ ἐδόθη ἡ τιμὴ καὶ βασιλεία
Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου

pass_b_english: Did he reach it? Clearly the Son reached into the glory of the Father. And how can we see this? He himself said next: “To him was given the honor and the kingdom” (Daniel 7:14). For he heard the Father saying, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (Psalm 110:1).

problems.why: Same inconsistency as above; Psalm 110:1 here vs. Psalm 109:1 in frag-rem-early for the identical quotation.
problems.fix: Standardize to one numbering system and note it.

problems.why: Same verse cited under two different psalm numbers across adjacent sections; reader may think two different passages are quoted.
problems.fix: Standardize numbering and add a note explaining the numbering system.

Three near-parallel fragments attribute the same Daniel quote to different speakers: 'the text,' 'he,' and 'Daniel himself.'
problems.fix: Standardize the attribution or note these are variant manuscript readings of the same passage.
